key_terms.meaning: P<sub>cr</sub> = π²EI/L<sub>e</sub>² is the axial load at which a straight elastic column first bows sideways.
L<sub>e</sub> = KL is the length of the equivalent pin-ended column, with K the effective-length factor for the end conditions.
λ = L<sub>e</sub>/r compares a column's effective length with its radius of gyration.
r = √(I/A), where I is second moment of area and A is cross-section area.
An empirical column formula, 1/P<sub>R</sub> = 1/P<sub>c</sub> + 1/P<sub>E</sub>, written P<sub>R</sub> = σ<sub>c</sub> A/(1 + aλ²), joining the crushing and Euler loads.
P<sub>c</sub> = σ<sub>c</sub> A is the load that would squash the column material in pure compression.
e is the offset of the axial load from the column centre line.
The bending due to a small eccentricity is multiplied by sec((π/2)√(P/P<sub>E</sub>)).
E<sub>t</sub> is the slope of the stress-strain curve after the proportional limit; E<sub>t</sub> < E.
σ<sub>prop</sub> is the stress above which stress is no longer proportional to strain; Euler buckling is valid only below it.
A member that carries axial compression and bending moment at the same time.
Approximately 1/(1 − P/P<sub>E</sub>) multiplies first-order bending moments in a beam-column.
σ1 is the largest normal stress on any plane through a point.
ε1 is the largest normal strain in any direction at a point.
τ<sub>max</sub> = (σ1 − σ3)/2 is the largest shear stress at a point.
σ<sub>v</sub> = √(σ1² − σ1σ2 + σ2²) for plane stress; yield occurs when σ<sub>v</sub> reaches σ<sub>y</sub>.
A plot of stress amplitude S against cycles to failure N, usually with N on a log scale.
σ<sub>e</sub> is the stress amplitude below which steel survives very many cycles; aluminium alloys show no true endurance limit.
σ<sub>m</sub> = (σ<sub>max</sub> + σ<sub>min</sub>)/2 is the steady part of a fluctuating stress.
σ<sub>a</sub> = (σ<sub>max</sub> − σ<sub>min</sub>)/2 is the half-range of a fluctuating stress.
σ<sub>cr</sub> = σ<sub>Y</sub> − (σ<sub>Y</sub>²/4π²E)λ² for intermediate columns, valid up to λ<sub>J</sub> = √(2π²E/σ<sub>Y</sub>).
σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>u</sub> = 1/n, the usual constant-life check with a mean stress.

takeaways: Euler load is a bifurcation load: a straight elastic column stays straight below it and bows above it.
Effective length turns fixed, pinned and free end conditions into an equivalent pin-ended column length.
Rankine-Gordon gives a smooth estimate for intermediate columns, between crushing load and Euler load.
Real columns have initial bow or load eccentricity, and the secant factor makes bending grow without limit at the Euler load.
Above the proportional limit the tangent modulus E<sub>t</sub> replaces E, so inelastic buckling occurs below the Euler load.
A beam-column must be designed with amplified moments because axial compression increases bending.
Maximum principal stress and maximum principal strain theories compare a complex stress state with a simple tension test.
For ductile metals, Tresca and von Mises criteria predict yield from shear or distortion, with Tresca usually conservative.
Repeated stress below yield can cause fatigue failure; the S-N curve gives cycles to failure at a given stress amplitude.
Mean and alternating stresses combine on a constant-life diagram to give a fatigue factor of safety.
bank_note: Long answers use the safe range of each column formula (check the proportional limit before Euler), the secant formula for imperfect struts, amplified moments for beam-columns, a principal-stress calculation before any yield criterion, and a constant-life diagram with a yield check for fatigue. Every answer closes with a numerical check.

bank.q: Define the Euler buckling load for a pin-ended column and explain the meaning of every term in P<sub>cr</sub> = π²EI/L<sub>e</sub>².
outline: State P<sub>cr</sub> = π²EI/L<sub>e</sub>².
Define E, I, L<sub>e</sub> and P<sub>cr</sub>.
Explain that the formula assumes elastic, straight, homogeneous column.
State that the column is stable below P<sub>cr</sub> and buckles above it.
answer: The formula. For a straight, pin-ended column of linear elastic material under a centred axial load, the Euler buckling load is

head: Symbol
Meaning
Unit
rows: axial load at which the straight shape stops being stable and a bowed shape is also in equilibrium
Young’s modulus of the material, a stiffness, not a strength
least second moment of area of the section (the column bows about its weakest axis)
effective length, KL; equal to L for pinned ends
comes from the first buckled shape, a half sine wave, kL = π

answer: Where it comes from. A small bow v(x) puts the load off the centroid, giving a moment Pv. Bending stiffness resists it: EIv″ = −Pv. With k² = P/EI the solution is v = C₁ sin kx; v(L) = 0 needs sin kL = 0, and the lowest non-zero root kL = π gives P = π²EI/L².

Meaning. Below Pcr a small disturbance dies away and the column straightens; at Pcr a bowed shape is also in equilibrium, so the column can bow with no extra side load. No strength term appears: two alloys with the same E and I buckle at the same load.
Assumptions. Initially straight; load through the centroid; material elastic up to buckling; small deflections; homogeneous and prismatic; ends that hold position and rotate freely.

answer.text: Worked number. Aluminium strut, pinned, L = 2.0 m, E = 70 GPa, I = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴, A = 500 mm².

answer: Closing check. The Euler stress π²E/λ² = 9.8696 × 70 000/100² = 69.1 MPa matches Pcr/A, and it is below the proportional limit, so the elastic formula holds for this strut.

bank.q: State the Rankine-Gordon formula and explain why it is used for intermediate columns instead of Euler load or crushing load alone.
outline: Write 1/P<sub>R</sub> = 1/P<sub>c</sub> + 1/P<sub>E</sub> or equivalent.
Define P<sub>c</sub> = σ<sub>c</sub> A and P<sub>E</sub> = π²EI/L<sub>e</sub>².
Explain short-column limit tends to crushing load.
Explain long-column limit tends to Euler load.
State that intermediate columns are neither fully squash nor fully elastic buckling.
answer: The formula. Rankine combined the crushing load Pc = σcA and the Euler load PE = π²EI/Le² as reciprocals:

answer.pre:
1/P<sub>R</sub> = 1/P<sub>c</sub> + 1/P<sub>E</sub>
P<sub>R</sub> = σ<sub>cA</sub>/(1 + aλ²),   a = σ<sub>c</sub>/(π²E),   λ = L<sub>e</sub>/r

answer: σ<sub>c</sub> is the crushing stress, A the area, r = √(I/A) the radius of gyration and a the Rankine constant (from tests in practice).

Why neither load alone will do. A short column crushes: Euler would give an enormous load and is unsafe. A long column buckles elastically: the crushing load would be unsafe. A column of middle slenderness bows a little and yields a little and fails below both, so a single formula that falls between them is needed.

The two limits. At λ → 0, aλ² → 0 and PR → σcA, the squash load. At large λ, aλ² ≫ 1 and PR → σcA/(aλ²) = π²EA/λ² = PE. The formula is an empirical fit built to pass through both ends; it always gives less than either.

answer.text: Worked number. Pinned steel strut, L = 600 mm, A = 400 mm², I = 1.0 × 10⁴ mm⁴, E = 200 GPa, σc = 320 MPa.

answer: Where it is used. Fuselage frame members, landing-gear braces and control linkages are often in this middle range. Design codes now use test-fitted column curves, but Rankine-Gordon remains the quick hand check.
Closing check. 1/128 + 1/54.8 = 0.00781 + 0.01825 = 0.02606, and 1/0.02606 = 38.4 kN, the same as the stress form; it lies below both 128 and 54.8 kN.

bank.q: Define maximum principal stress theory and maximum principal strain theory. For plane stress, write expressions for principal stresses from σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub> and τ<sub>xy</sub>.
outline: State σ1 = (σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>)/2 + √(((σ<sub>x</sub> − σ<sub>y</sub>)/2)² + τ<sub>xy</sub>²).
State σ2 = (σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>)/2 − √(((σ<sub>x</sub> − σ<sub>y</sub>)/2)² + τ<sub>xy</sub>²).
Maximum principal stress theory: safe if σ₁ ≤ tensile strength and |σ₃| ≤ compressive strength.
Maximum principal strain theory: safe if largest principal strain is below yield strain in tension test.
Use ε1 = (σ1 − νσ2)/E for plane stress.
answer: Principal stresses. For plane stress σx, σy, τxy:

answer.pre:
σ₁, σ₂ = (σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>)/2 ± √[((σ<sub>x</sub> − σ<sub>y</sub>)/2)² + τ<sub>xy</sub>²]
σ₃ = 0 (the free surface)

answer: Maximum principal stress theory (Rankine). Failure starts when the largest tensile principal stress reaches the tensile strength from a simple test, or the most compressive one reaches the compressive strength: safe while σ₁ ≤ σYt and |σ₃| ≤ σYc. Shear is ignored. It suits brittle materials, which crack on the plane of largest tension.
Maximum principal strain theory (St Venant). Failure starts when the largest principal strain reaches the strain at yield in a tension test, σY/E. For plane stress

answer.pre:
Eε₁ = σ₁ − νσ₂     Eε₂ = σ₂ − νσ₁     Eε₃ = −ν(σ₁ + σ₂)
safe while max(|Eε₁|, |Eε₂|, |Eε₃|) ≤ σ<sub>Y</sub>

answer.text: Worked numbers. σx = 100 MPa, σy = −40 MPa, τxy = 30 MPa, σY = 250 MPa, ν = 0.30.

answer: Comparing. The strain theory gives the lower factor here because the compressive σ₂ adds Poisson stretch along σ₁. For a ductile metal both are unsafe under shear: in pure shear Rankine predicts failure at τ = σY and St Venant at σY/1.3 = 0.77σY, while the metal yields near 0.58σY.
Closing check. σ₁ + σ₂ = 60 MPa = σx + σy, and σ₁σ₂ = −4900 = σx × σy − τxy² = −4000 − 900, so the principal stresses are right.

bank.q: Explain what an S-N curve shows and define endurance limit. State how aluminium alloys differ from steels in this respect.
outline: S-N curve plots stress amplitude S against cycles to failure N.
Usually N is on logarithmic scale.
Higher stress amplitude gives shorter fatigue life.
Endurance limit is stress amplitude below which steel survives very many cycles.
Aluminium alloys do not show a true endurance limit; fatigue life continues to depend on stress amplitude.
answer: What the curve shows. An S-N (Wöhler) curve plots the stress amplitude S of a repeated cycle against the number of cycles N to failure, with N on a logarithmic scale. The basic curve is for a fully reversed cycle (mean stress zero), as in a rotating-bending test.
Shape. The higher the amplitude, the shorter the life. On log axes the sloping part is close to a straight line, Basquin’s law S = ANb with b negative.

answer.text: Worked numbers. A steel gives 600 MPa at 10³ cycles and 400 MPa at 10⁶ cycles.

answer: Endurance limit. For many steels the curve flattens beyond about 10⁶ to 10⁷ cycles. The amplitude of that flat part is the endurance (fatigue) limit Se: below it the specimen survives indefinitely. In the example Se = 400 MPa, read from the test, not assumed from the ultimate strength.

Aluminium alloys. They show no true endurance limit; the curve keeps falling at long lives. Their fatigue strength is quoted at a stated life, often 5 × 10⁸ cycles. An aluminium wing skin therefore has a finite fatigue life at any stress amplitude, and its design life comes from the S-N curve and the load spectrum, with inspections.

Real parts. Surface finish, size, notches, corrosion and mean stress lower the curve: with surface 0.80, size 0.85 and reliability 0.90 factors, a 400 MPa specimen limit becomes 244.8 MPa for the part.
Closing check. 900 × (2.23 × 10⁴)−0.0587 = 900 × 0.556 = 500 MPa, so the fitted law reproduces the stress.

bank.q: A pin-ended aluminium strut is 2.0 m long, E = 70 GPa, I = 1.2×10⁻⁶ m⁴ and A = 600 mm². Calculate the Euler load and slenderness ratio. If yield strength is 250 MPa, decide whether Euler or Rankine-Gordon is more appropriate.
outline: Use L<sub>e</sub> = L for pin-ended column.
Compute P<sub>E</sub> = π²EI/L².
Compute r = √(I/A).
Compute λ = L/r.
Compare P<sub>E</sub>/A with yield strength.
State that a very slender column is Euler-like; an intermediate column needs Rankine-Gordon.
answer: Section. Pinned, so Le = L = 2.0 m. E = 70 GPa, I = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, A = 600 mm² = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ m².

Is Euler valid? The Euler stress, 345.4 MPa, is above the 250 MPa yield strength, so it is above the proportional limit too. The limiting slenderness for Euler with σprop ≈ 200 MPa is √(π² × 70 000/200) = 58.8, and λ = 44.7 is below it. The strut is intermediate, and Euler would overestimate its strength.

Johnson check. λJ = √(2π²E/σY) = 74.3, so Johnson applies: σcr = 250 − 250²/(4π² × 70 000) × 2000 = 250 − 45.2 = 204.8 MPa, P = 122.9 kN. The theoretical Rankine constant gives the lower, more conservative 87.0 kN; a test value of a would bring it closer to Johnson.
Decision. Use Rankine-Gordon (or an inelastic column formula), not Euler. Euler’s 207.3 kN is 2.4 times the Rankine load and would be unsafe.
Closing check. 1/150 + 1/207.3 = 0.006667 + 0.004824 = 0.011491, giving 87.0 kN again; it is below both the squash load 150 kN and the Euler load.

bank.q: A column of length 3.0 m is fixed at both ends. Take K = 0.5, E = 200 GPa and I = 8.0×10⁻⁶ m⁴. Calculate the effective length and Euler buckling load.
outline: Use L<sub>e</sub> = KL = 0.5 × 3.0 m.
Obtain L<sub>e</sub> = 1.5 m.
Use P<sub>cr</sub> = π²EI/L<sub>e</sub>².
Substitute E and I in consistent units.
State final load in kN.
answer: Effective length. Both ends fixed: K = 0.5, so Le = 0.5 × 3.0 = 1.5 m.
Why 0.5. The fixed-fixed buckled shape is a full cosine wave over L; between the points of contraflexure at L/4 and 3L/4 it is a pinned half-wave of length L/2.

answer.text: Euler load. E = 200 GPa = 200 × 10⁹ Pa, I = 8.0 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴.

answer: Validity must be checked. The area is not given. If the column were, say, A = 4000 mm², the Euler stress would be 7.018 × 10⁶/4.0 × 10⁻³ = 1755 MPa, far above any structural steel’s yield. Then r = √(8×10⁻⁶/4×10⁻³) = 44.7 mm and λ = 1500/44.7 = 33.5, a stocky column that would crush or fail inelastically long before 7018 kN. Euler is valid only when λ exceeds about 99 for mild steel.
Closing check. The fixed-fixed load is four times the pinned load (4 × 1755 = 7020 kN), as K = 0.5 requires.

bank.q: A strut has a small load eccentricity e. Derive or state the secant formula and use it to find the maximum compressive stress for given P, e, A, I, E and L.
outline: Maximum stress = P/A + (P e c/I) sec((π/2)√(P/P<sub>E</sub>)).
Define c as distance from neutral axis to extreme fibre.
Define P<sub>E</sub> = π²EI/L².
Explain that secant factor grows as P approaches P<sub>E</sub>.
Substitute numerical values carefully with units.
answer: Set-up. A pinned strut of length L carries P at an eccentricity e at both ends. With deflection v from the chord, the moment is M = P(e + v), so

answer.pre:
EIv″ + Pv = −Pe,   k² = P/EI
v = e[cos kx + tan(kL/2) sin kx − 1]
mid-span: v = e[sec(kL/2) − 1],   M<sub>max</sub> = Pe sec(kL/2)

answer.text: Secant formula. Adding direct and bending stress with Z = I/c and I = Ar²:
answer.pre: σ<sub>max</sub> = P/A + Pe c sec(kL/2)/I = (P/A)[1 + (ec/r²) sec((π/2)√(P/P<sub>E</sub>))]

answer: c is the distance from the centroid to the extreme compressive fibre and P<sub>E</sub> = π²EI/L<sub>e</sub>². The argument is in radians; sec grows without limit as P → P<sub>E</sub>.

answer.text: Numbers. Pinned aluminium strut, L = 1.0 m, E = 70 GPa, A = 200 mm², I = 2.0 × 10⁴ mm⁴, c = 10 mm, e = 2 mm, P = 8 kN.

answer: Meaning. The mean stress is 40 MPa but the peak is 61.8 MPa, 1.55 times larger. Without amplification the bending stress would be 40 × 0.20 = 8 MPa; the secant makes it 21.8 MPa. Ignoring the bending would understate the peak by 35 %.
Common slip. Using degrees: cos 1.195° = 0.9998 gives sec ≈ 1 and a wrong 48 MPa.
Closing check. P/PE = 0.579; (π/2)√0.579 = 1.195 rad, the same argument written the other way, so both forms agree.

bank.q: A simply supported beam-column carries axial compression P = 0.3P<sub>E</sub> and a transverse load giving first-order midspan moment M0 = 12 kN m. Calculate the amplified moment and maximum bending stress if the section modulus is Z = 150 cm³.
outline: Use amplification factor ≈ 1/(1 − P/P<sub>E</sub>).
Compute factor = 1/(1 − 0.3) = 1.43 approximately.
Amplified moment = 1.43 × 12 kN m.
Bending stress = M/Z.
State that axial stress P/A must be added for the peak compressive stress.
answer: Amplification. Axial compression acting on the deflected beam adds a moment Pv, so the first-order moment M₀ is magnified. For a sine-shaped moment the factor is exact; for a transverse load it is a safe estimate:
Without amplification it would be 12 × 10⁶/150 × 10³ = 80.0 MPa, so the axial load adds 43 % to the bending stress.
Axial stress. The total compressive stress adds P/A on the compression face. With PE not given in kN, P/A cannot be found here; it must be added once A and P are known.
Exact factor for a central point load. tan u/u with u = (π/2)√0.3 = 0.860 rad gives 1.351, so Mmax = 16.21 kN·m and σb = 108.1 MPa. The simple factor, 1.429, is about 6 % on the safe side.
Closing check. 17.14/12 = 1.429 and 114.3/80.0 = 1.429: the stress grows in the same ratio as the moment.

bank.q: For plane stress, σ<sub>x</sub> = 100 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 40 MPa and τ<sub>xy</sub> = 30 MPa. Find principal stresses, maximum shear stress and von Mises stress. Compare with a yield strength σ<sub>Y</sub> = 250 MPa using Tresca and von Mises.
outline: Compute centre = (σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>)/2 = 70 MPa.
Compute radius = √(((σ<sub>x</sub> − σ<sub>y</sub>)/2)² + τ<sub>xy</sub>²).
Principal stresses from centre ± radius.
τ<sub>max</sub> = (σ₁ − σ₃)/2 with σ₃ = 0, since both in-plane principal stresses are tensile.
von Mises stress for plane stress: √(σ1² − σ1σ2 + σ2²).
Check Tresca: 2τ<sub>max</sub> below σ<sub>Y</sub>; check von Mises: σ<sub>vM</sub> below σ<sub>Y</sub>.

answer.pre:
centre = (100 + 40)/2 = 70 MPa
radius = √(30² + 30²) = 42.43 MPa
σ₁ = 112.43 MPa,  σ₂ = 27.57 MPa,  σ₃ = 0

answer: Maximum shear stress. Both in-plane principal stresses are tensile, so the largest shear is not (σ₁ − σ₂)/2 = 42.43 MPa but involves σ₃ = 0:

answer.pre:
σ<sub>vM</sub> = √(σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂²) = √(12 640 − 3100 + 760) = √10 301 = 101.5 MPa
check: √(σ<sub>x</sub>² − σ<sub>x</sub>σ_y + σ<sub>y</sub>² + 3τ<sub>xy</sub>²) = √(10 000 − 4000 + 1600 + 2700) = 101.5 MPa

answer: Comment. Tresca is the conservative check and gives 2.22. The common slip, using σ₁ − σ₂ when both are tensile, would overstate the margin by a third.
Closing check. σ₁ + σ₂ = 140 = σx + σy and σ₁σ₂ = 3100 = 100 × 40 − 30², so the principal stresses are right.

bank.q: A component sees σ<sub>max</sub> = 120 MPa and σ<sub>min</sub> = 20 MPa. Find mean stress, alternating stress and stress ratio. Mark the point on a Goodman diagram and find the safety factor if σ<sub>e</sub> = 160 MPa and σ<sub>u</sub> = 400 MPa.
outline: R = σ<sub>min</sub>/σ<sub>max</sub> = 20/120 = 0.167.
Goodman line: σ<sub>a</sub>/σ<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/σ<sub>u</sub> = 1 at failure.
Safety factor n from (σ<sub>a</sub>/σ<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/σ<sub>u</sub>) = 1/n.

answer.pre:
σ<sub>m</sub> = (120 + 20)/2 = 70 MPa
σ<sub>a</sub> = (120 − 20)/2 = 50 MPa
R = σ<sub>min</sub>/σ<sub>max</sub> = 20/120 = 0.167
A = σ<sub>a</sub>/σ<sub>m</sub> = 50/70 = 0.714

answer: Goodman diagram. Plot σm across and σa up. The Goodman line joins σe = 160 MPa on the σa axis to σu = 400 MPa on the σm axis. The load point (70, 50) lies below it.

answer.text: Factor of safety. Scale both stresses by n until the point reaches the line:

answer: Yield check. σmax = 120 MPa is far below any structural yield strength, so first-cycle yielding is not a concern.
Without mean stress. If the mean were ignored, n = σe/σa = 160/50 = 3.2, overstating the margin by 56 %. The tensile mean stress uses up part of the fatigue strength.
Closing check. σm + σa = 120 = σmax and σm − σa = 20 = σmin.

bank.q: Compare Euler, Rankine-Gordon and tangent-modulus approaches for short, intermediate and long columns. Explain which is appropriate for an aircraft strut with initial bow.
outline: Short column: yielding or crushing dominates.
Intermediate column: Rankine-Gordon or tangent-modulus approach.
Long slender column: Euler buckling dominates.
Initial bow or eccentricity makes secant amplification important.
Tangent modulus applies after proportional limit.
Aircraft strut design must consider imperfection, end fixity and material non-linearity.
answer: Three regimes. Short columns crush or yield; long columns buckle elastically; intermediate columns bow and yield together and fail below both predictions.

answer.text: Numbers for one alloy. E = 70 GPa, σY = 320 MPa (stresses in MPa; Rankine uses the theoretical a).

answer: Euler. Valid only when the buckling stress is below the proportional limit (λ above about 59 for this alloy). It is exact for a perfect elastic column and unsafe for short ones.

Rankine-Gordon. A single empirical curve from the squash load to the Euler load. Simple and always below both; with the theoretical constant it is conservative at middle λ (183.8 against 260.7 MPa at λ = 40). Test constants improve it.

Tangent modulus (and Johnson). Physically based for the inelastic range: Et replaces E above the proportional limit, and Shanley showed buckling starts at the tangent-modulus load. Johnson’s parabola is a closed-form fit to it, valid up to λJ.

Aircraft strut with an initial bow. None of the three alone is enough. A bow a acts like an eccentricity: the secant formula gives the peak stress, for example a 1 m aluminium strut with a 2 mm offset reaching 61.8 MPa at a mean stress of 40 MPa. The recommended route: (1) find Le for the real end fittings; (2) compute λ and pick Euler or the tangent-modulus/Johnson strength for the perfect column; (3) check the bowed strut by the secant formula against the proportional limit or yield; (4) apply the design factor. For an intermediate strut, the secant check with the tangent-modulus strength governs.
Closing check. At λJ = 65.7, Johnson and Euler both give 160.1 MPa = σY/2, so the column curve is continuous.

bank.q: Explain why a beam-column must be designed with amplified moments. Discuss how axial compression changes stiffness and when second-order effects become large.
outline: Axial compression reduces lateral stiffness.
First-order moment M0 is multiplied by approximately 1/(1 − P/P<sub>E</sub>).
Amplification grows rapidly as P approaches P<sub>E</sub>.
Maximum stress combines P/A and amplified bending stress.
Second-order effects are important for slender members and high axial load.
Design must check stability, not only material strength.
answer: Why the moment grows. In a beam-column the axial load P acts on the deflected shape, adding Pv to the first-order moment M₀. The extra moment deflects the member further, which adds more moment.

Stiffness view. Compression lowers the effective bending stiffness. For a sine-shaped mode the lateral stiffness falls in proportion to (1 − P/PE) and reaches zero at the Euler load, which is buckling.

answer.pre:
M<sub>max</sub> ≈ M₀/(1 − P/P<sub>E</sub>)
exact for a sine moment; equal end moments: M₀ sec((π/2)√(P/P<sub>E</sub>))

answer: Worked case. A 1.0 m aluminium stringer (EI = 2520 N·m², PE = 24.9 kN) at P = 15 kN has P/PE = 0.603 and factor 2.52. A 50 N·m side-load moment becomes 126 N·m; with A = 250 mm², I = 3.6 × 10⁴ mm⁴ and c = 12 mm the peak stress is 60.0 + 42.0 = 102.0 MPa, where a first-order check would give 76.7 MPa.

When second-order effects become large. Below P/PE ≈ 0.1 the increase is about 10 % and can often be ignored. Above 0.3 it exceeds 40 %, and above 0.5 the moment more than doubles. Slender members (large Le/r), heavy axial load, and loose end fixity (larger Le, smaller PE) all push P/PE up.

Design consequence. Use the amplified moment in the interaction check P/Pcr + M/Mu ≤ 1, and keep P well below PE. A member can fail in combined compression and bending at a load far below both its squash load and its Euler load, so stability must be checked, not only material strength.

bank.q: Compare Tresca, von Mises and octahedral shear criteria for ductile aircraft metals. Why do Tresca and von Mises bracket experimental yield?
outline: Tresca uses maximum shear stress = (σ1 − σ3)/2.
von Mises uses distortion energy or equivalent stress.
Octahedral shear stress is proportional to von Mises stress.
Tresca is generally conservative.
von Mises usually agrees better with ductile metal tests.
Experimental yield lies between or near these predictions depending on stress state.

answer.pre:
Tresca:     max|σᵢ − σⱼ| = σ<sub>Y</sub>          (largest shear = σ<sub>Y</sub>/2)
von Mises:  √{[(σ₁−σ₂)² + (σ₂−σ₃)² + (σ₃−σ₁)²]/2} = σ<sub>Y</sub>
octahedral: τ<sub>oct</sub> = (1/3)√[(σ₁−σ₂)² + (σ₂−σ₃)² + (σ₃−σ₁)²] = (√2/3)σ<sub>Y</sub>

answer: Octahedral and von Mises are one criterion. σvM = (3/√2)τoct exactly, so yield at τoct = (√2/3)σY is von Mises written on the octahedral plane. Both depend only on distortion; hydrostatic stress changes volume and causes no yield in either.

answer.text: How far apart Tresca and von Mises are. Equivalent stresses (MPa):

answer: Why they bracket test data. Both are calibrated on the tension test, so they agree there and under equal biaxial stress. They differ most in shear: Tresca predicts shear yield at 0.50σY, von Mises at 0.577σY. Tests on ductile metals (thin tubes under tension and torsion) give shear yield between 0.5 and 0.6σY, usually close to 0.577. So test points lie on or just inside the von Mises ellipse and outside the Tresca hexagon: Tresca is the lower bound, von Mises the better fit.

For aircraft metals. Aluminium alloys, titanium and steels used in fittings, spars and frames are ductile, so von Mises is the normal design criterion and the default output of finite element codes. Tresca is used as a quick, conservative hand check, at most 15.5 % more conservative.
Worked factors. For σx = 100, σy = −40, τxy = 30 MPa and σY = 250 MPa: Tresca 250/152.3 = 1.64; von Mises and octahedral 250/135.3 = 1.85 (τoct = 63.77 MPa, (3/√2) × 63.77 = 135.3).
Closing check. 152.3/135.3 = 1.126, inside the 1.0 to 1.155 range that the two criteria can differ by.

bank.q: A fatigue-critical aircraft fitting has mean stress and alternating stress. Discuss how stress ratio, mean stress and surface condition affect fatigue life, and explain the use of a constant-life diagram for safety factor.
outline: Stress ratio R = σ<sub>min</sub>/σ<sub>max</sub> describes the cycle.
Tensile mean stress usually reduces fatigue life.
Alternating stress drives fatigue damage.
Surface finish, stress concentration and environment affect fatigue strength.
Constant-life diagram plots σ<sub>a</sub> against σ<sub>m</sub> for a chosen life.
Goodman or similar line gives safety factor against fatigue failure.
answer: Stress ratio and the cycle. R = σmin/σmax describes the cycle: R = −1 fully reversed, R = 0 zero to maximum, R near 1 nearly steady. For σmax = 300 MPa and σmin = −100 MPa, σm = 100 MPa, σa = 200 MPa and R = −0.33.

Mean stress. A tensile mean stress opens cracks and shortens life at the same amplitude; a compressive mean helps (though it is not counted on in design). The alternating part drives crack growth, but the mean decides how much amplitude the part can take.

Surface condition. Cracks start at the surface. Machining marks, corrosion pits, fretting and notches lower the endurance limit; shot peening and polishing raise it. In numbers, surface 0.80, size 0.85 and reliability 0.90 factors reduce a 400 MPa specimen limit to 244.8 MPa.

answer.text: Constant-life diagram. σm across, σa up. The Goodman line joins Se to Su, Soderberg Se to Sy, Gerber is a parabola through Se and Su, and Langer σa + σm = Sy marks first-cycle yield. Scaling both stresses by n until the point reaches a line gives the factor of safety.

answer: Reading it. A rougher surface pulls Se down and every fatigue factor falls with it, while the yield line does not move. The fitting is safe by Goodman (1.60 polished, 1.33 machined), and the yield check passes, σmax = 300 MPa < 600 MPa.

In aircraft practice. Real fittings see a spectrum of cycles, so the diagram is used with a load spectrum, Miner’s rule and damage-tolerance inspections; but the single-cycle factor shows at once how mean stress and surface finish move the margin.

glossary.def: Sudden lateral deflection of a slender member under axial compression when the load reaches a critical value.
A structural member loaded mainly along its axis in compression.
The load at which a perfect column first becomes unstable in a chosen buckling mode.
The length of an equivalent pin-ended column that buckles at the same load as the real column.
The ratio L<sub>e</sub>/r, used to classify a column as short, intermediate or long.
A section property r = √(I/A) that measures how far the area is spread from the centroid.
An empirical formula that combines crushing load and Euler load for intermediate columns.
An axial load whose line of action does not pass through the centroid of the section.
A formula for maximum stress in an eccentrically loaded column, containing sec((π/2)√(P/P<sub>E</sub>)).
The local slope of the stress-strain curve after the proportional limit.
The highest stress for which stress remains proportional to strain.
A member carrying axial compression together with bending moment.
The increase of bending moment in a beam-column caused by axial compression acting on lateral deflection.
A normal stress on a plane where shear stress is zero.
A normal strain along a principal direction, where shear strain is zero.
A rule that predicts the stress state at which a material begins to yield.
A yield criterion based on maximum shear stress reaching the value at yield in tension.
A yield criterion based on distortion energy reaching the value at yield in tension.
Shear stress on the octahedral plane; it is proportional to the von Mises equivalent stress.
Failure by repeated or fluctuating stress at levels below the static yield strength.
A graph of stress amplitude against number of cycles to failure.
The fully reversed stress amplitude below which a steel survives indefinitely; aluminium alloys have none and are quoted at a fixed life.
The average of maximum and minimum stress in a fatigue cycle.
Half the difference between maximum and minimum stress in a fatigue cycle.
R = σ<sub>min</sub>/σ<sub>max</sub>, a measure of how a fatigue cycle is biased.
A constant-life diagram plotting alternating stress against mean stress with a straight failure line.
